author: ohtadmin
title: TV reporter details storm from home
text:
Talk about your eyewitness news.
Jamestown residents watching the WJAR news throughout the historic Feb. 22-23 blizzard may have noticed a familiar face reporting from their hometown.
John Perik reported from his family’s house at the eastern terminus of High Street to keep viewers informed about the weather and surf conditions on Narragansett Bay.
“There’s something to be said about reporting in your hometown,” he said.
Perik filmed his live reports on his smartphone and sent them to Providence using a real-time reporting application. The station broadcast his clips of waves crashing ashore as it snowed with barely any visibility of the Pell Bridge or Bay View complex behind him.
His report included showing his neighbors’ flagpole “uprooted at the base,” which “went crashing down this afternoon,” and his Uncle Doug and Aunt Martha “digging their car out.”
“You kind of forget the magnitude of a storm like this until you’re in the middle of it,” Perik said. “Just watching the snow build up in a matter of minutes, it’s a spectacle.”
Perik joined NBC 10 in June 2024. He is an evening general assignment reporter and fills in at the anchor desk on weekends and holidays. The blizzard was not the first time he reported from his hometown.
Perik covered the story when a bus blew a tire and flipped onto its side on Route 138 near the toll plaza in September 2025. He also reported on the closure of Zeek’s Creek in October 2024 and from Beavertail State Park for stories on the Revolution Wind turbine farm.
“I always love reporting in Jamestown,” he said. “It’s a town that means so much to me. Whenever I can say, ‘Reporting live from Jamestown for NBC 10 News,’ that’s the best way to tag out of a report.”
Perik said he does not ordinarily use his phone to take video, but he used what he had available given the conditions and magnitude of the storm. Because there were other NBC 10 reporters who also were reporting during the blizzard, he decided to focus on the coast, which no one else was doing.
“I wanted to give our viewers an understanding what it looks like by the water,” he said. “You can hear the winds screeching. It was a bit of an eerie noise when you’re by the water and the wind. It’s the spectacle of Mother Nature.”
Perik filmed four live broadcasts during the blizzard and, after signing off, heard immediate reactions from his parents at home.
Perik, originally from East Greenwich, was raised in Jamestown and has lived on the island for most of his life. He attended the Wheeler School in Providence and graduated from Portsmouth Abbey in 2020.
While at Portsmouth Abbey, Perik hosted a sports talk show on the school’s radio station. He also interned for the Newport Gulls baseball team in the summer of 2018, where he was the team’s director of marketing and on-field emcee. Perik said the opportunity with the Gulls gave him the self-assurance to pursue his career in television news.
“If you want to be a news reporter, it is cutthroat, it is competitive every single day,” he said. “There really is no off day. You have to be sharp and you have to bring 100% to each story you do. The Newport Gulls gave me a level of confidence that has propelled me to where I am right now.”
After high school, Perik attended Syracuse University, where he graduated in 2024 with a degree in broadcast journalism. At Syracuse, Perik was a reporter and anchor for the school’s Citrus TV network and won the 2024 White House News Photographer Association’s “Eyes of History” contest and the 2024 Hearst Television Features Competition.
Perik interned during his sophomore year in 2022 at WCVB NewsCenter 5 in Boston and NBC 10, where he was hired in a part-time role in December 2023 until he eventually was offered a fulltime position seven months later.
Perik said it has been “a great experience” working for the “same news station that I’ve watched my entire life.” He called it a “dream come true” to be part of the NBC newsroom.

His report included showing his neighbors’ flagpole “uprooted at the base,” which “went crashing down this afternoon,” and his Uncle Doug and Aunt Martha “digging their car out.” “You kind of forget the magnitude of a storm like this until you’re in the middle of it,” Perik said.
